summary.title: The Red Flags on Your Resume
summary.one_liner: Learn which resume habits (noise, fluff phrases, skill graphics, long text blocks, overused links, unprofessional photos) make recruiters reject candidates, and what to put in their place.
takeaways: Aim for a one-page resume (more is acceptable, but key info belongs on page one) and break text into short, spaced sections.
Focus work experience on outcomes and delivered value with defensible data points, not lists of libraries or 'clean code' claims.
Use 'I' to show your individual contribution instead of only 'we' and 'team'.
Skip skill bars/graphs, vague fluff, and link dumps unless each link has context and works; keep interests only when they are relevant or unique.
Get resumes reviewed by recruiters or HR, since a red flag in the first 100ms can create lasting negative bias.
summary.summary: The author, a software engineer who has reviewed hundreds of resumes, explains the red flags recruiters notice and the reasoning behind each one. The post uses a 'signals vs noise' framing, with a metric of signals per line, and covers length, text density, first impressions, spelling, fluff phrases, work experience focus, skill graphics, libraries lists, education, photos, interests, design, and getting outside reviews. It is written as an opinion-based essay with practical examples rather than a step-by-step guide. Specific resources mentioned include the Hemingway Editor, Ann Handley's 'Everybody Writes', and a Resume Genius article.
